5.2 Reliable Byte Stream (TCP)

In contrast to a simple demultiplexing protocol like UDP, a more sophisticated transport protocol is one that offers a reliable, connection-oriented, byte-stream service. Such a service has proven useful to a wide assortment of applications because it frees the application from having to worry about missing or reordered data. The Internet’s Transmission Control Protocol is probably the most widely used protocol of this type; it is also the most carefully tuned. It is for these two reasons that this section studies TCP in detail, although we identify and discuss alternative design choices at the end of the section.

In terms of the properties of transport protocols given in the problem statement at the start of this chapter, TCP guarantees the reliable, in-order delivery of a stream of bytes. It is a full-duplex protocol, meaning that each TCP connection supports a pair of byte streams, one flowing in each direction. It also includes a flow-control mechanism for each of these byte streams that allows the receiver to limit how much data the sender can transmit at a given time. Finally, like UDP, TCP supports a demultiplexing mechanism that allows multiple application programs on any given host to simultaneously carry on a conversation with their peers.

TCP is a byte-oriented protocol, which means that the sender writes bytes into a TCP connection and the receiver reads bytes out of the TCP connection. Although “byte stream” describes the service TCP offers to application processes, TCP does not, itself, transmit individual bytes over the Internet. Instead, TCP on the source host buffers enough bytes from the sending process to fill a reasonably sized packet and then sends this packet to its peer on the destination host. TCP on the destination host then empties the contents of the packet into a receive buffer, and the receiving process reads from this buffer at its leisure. This situation is illustrated in Figure 127, which, for simplicity, shows data flowing in only one direction. Remember that, in general, a single TCP connection supports byte streams flowing in both directions.

The packets exchanged between TCP peers in Figure 127 are called segments, since each one carries a segment of the byte stream. Each TCP segment contains the header schematically depicted in Figure 128. The relevance of most of these fields will become apparent throughout this section. For now, we simply introduce them.

In addition to the above features, TCP also implements a highly tuned congestion-control mechanism. The idea of this mechanism is to throttle how fast TCP sends data, not for the sake of keeping the sender from over-running the receiver, but so as to keep the sender from overloading the network. A description of TCP’s congestion-control mechanism is postponed until the next chapter, where we discuss it in the larger context of how network resources are fairly allocated.

To see how the sending and receiving sides of TCP interact with each other to implement reliable and ordered delivery, consider the situation illustrated in Figure 132. TCP on the sending side maintains a send buffer. This buffer is used to store data that has been sent but not yet acknowledged, as well as data that has been written by the sending application but not transmitted. On the receiving side, TCP maintains a receive buffer. This buffer holds data that arrives out of order, as well as data that is in the correct order (i.e., there are no missing bytes earlier in the stream) but that the application process has not yet had the chance to read.

questions.stem:
Consider the service TCP offers to application processes and the units TCP exchanges with its peer.

1. The service is reliable, in-order, and full-duplex.
2. Each connection supports a pair of byte streams, one in each direction.
3. TCP is byte-oriented: the sender writes bytes into the connection, and the receiver reads bytes out of it.
4. TCP itself does not transmit individual bytes over the Internet.
5. TCP buffers bytes at the source until it can form a reasonably sized packet, sends that packet to its peer, and the destination TCP empties the packet into a receive buffer for the receiving process to read at its leisure.
6. The packets exchanged between TCP peers are called segments, and each carries a segment of the byte stream.

In your own words, describe the reliable, ordered, full-duplex byte-stream service that TCP offers applications, and explain how it differs from the segments TCP actually exchanges across the Internet.
questions.answer:
TCP offers applications a reliable, in-order, full-duplex byte-stream service: the sender writes bytes into the connection and the receiver reads bytes out of it, with reliable, in-order delivery, and each connection supports a pair of byte streams, one flowing in each direction.

This service is distinct from what TCP transmits: TCP does not send individual bytes across the Internet. Instead, the source TCP buffers enough bytes to form a reasonably sized packet and sends that packet to its peer; the destination TCP empties the packet into a receive buffer, and the receiving process reads from that buffer at its leisure. These exchanged packets are called segments, and each segment carries a segment of the byte stream.
questions.explanation:
The application sees a byte stream: bytes in, bytes out, reliably and in order, in both directions.

The network sees segments: TCP buffers bytes, forms reasonably sized packets, and exchanges those segments between peers; the receiver buffers the segment contents for the application to read.

So the byte stream is the service interface to applications, while segments are the units TCP actually transmits.

TCP gives an application process a reliable, ordered, full-duplex byte-stream service. That means an application writes bytes into its end of a TCP connection and the receiving application reads bytes out of the other end as a continuous stream, not as a sequence of messages or records. TCP guarantees that bytes are delivered reliably and in the same order in which they were written, despite loss, duplication, or reordering in the underlying Internet. Because TCP is full-duplex, one connection supports two independent byte streams, one in each direction, and each direction has its own flow control and reliability mechanisms. The byte-stream abstraction also hides packet boundaries: if the sender performs one write of 100 bytes, the receiver may need several reads to consume all 100 bytes, or if the sender performs several small writes, the receiver may read them together in one larger read. TCP does not preserve application write boundaries.

Internally, however, TCP does not transmit individual bytes across the Internet. The sending TCP buffers bytes written by the application until it has enough data to form a reasonably sized packet. It then sends that packet, called a TCP segment, to the peer TCP. A segment carries a portion of the byte stream plus TCP header fields such as sequence numbers, acknowledgment numbers, flags, and window information. The receiving TCP places the segment's data into a receive buffer and delivers bytes to the receiving application in order, at the application's pace. Thus the segments are the actual units exchanged between TCP peers, while the reliable, ordered, full-duplex byte stream is the service interface TCP presents to applications. The application sees a stream of bytes; the network sees TCP segments carrying pieces of that stream.

Consider the service TCP offers to application processes and the units TCP exchanges with its peer.

1. The service is reliable, in-order, and full-duplex.
2. Each connection supports a pair of byte streams, one in each direction.
3. TCP is byte-oriented: the sender writes bytes into the connection, and the receiver reads bytes out of it.
4. TCP itself does not transmit individual bytes over the Internet.
5. TCP buffers bytes at the source until it can form a reasonably sized packet, sends that packet to its peer, and the destination TCP empties the packet into a receive buffer for the receiving process to read at its leisure.
6. The packets exchanged between TCP peers are called segments, and each carries a segment of the byte stream.

In your own words, describe the reliable, ordered, full-duplex byte-stream service that TCP offers applications, and explain how it differs from the segments TCP actually exchanges across the Internet.

TCP offers applications a reliable, in-order, full-duplex byte-stream service: the sender writes bytes into the connection and the receiver reads bytes out of it, with reliable, in-order delivery, and each connection supports a pair of byte streams, one flowing in each direction.

This service is distinct from what TCP transmits: TCP does not send individual bytes across the Internet. Instead, the source TCP buffers enough bytes to form a reasonably sized packet and sends that packet to its peer; the destination TCP empties the packet into a receive buffer, and the receiving process reads from that buffer at its leisure. These exchanged packets are called segments, and each segment carries a segment of the byte stream.

Consider the following description from the course material about the service TCP offers to applications.

"TCP guarantees the reliable, in-order delivery of a stream of bytes. It is a full-duplex protocol, meaning that each TCP connection supports a pair of byte streams, one flowing in each direction. ... TCP is a byte-oriented protocol, which means that the sender writes bytes into a TCP connection and the receiver reads bytes out of the TCP connection. Although 'byte stream' describes the service TCP offers to application processes, TCP does not, itself, transmit individual bytes over the Internet. Instead, TCP on the source host buffers enough bytes from the sending process to fill a reasonably sized packet and then sends this packet to its peer on the destination host."

1. A sending application writes a sequence of bytes into the connection.
2. The receiving application reads bytes from the connection.

Question: In your own words, describe the reliable, ordered, full-duplex byte-stream service that TCP offers applications, and explain how it differs from the way TCP transmits data across the network using segments.
questions.answer:
TCP offers applications a reliable, ordered, full-duplex byte-stream service. This means the sender writes bytes into the connection and the receiver reads bytes out of it, with TCP guaranteeing that the bytes are delivered reliably and in order, and that each connection supports a pair of byte streams flowing in opposite directions at the same time.

This differs from how TCP transmits data across the network: TCP does not send individual bytes. Instead, the source host buffers enough bytes from the sending process to fill a reasonably sized packet and sends that packet as a segment to its peer. The destination host empties the segment's contents into a receive buffer, and the receiving application reads from that buffer at its leisure.

TCP gives the application a reliable, ordered byte stream: the sending process writes bytes into the connection and the receiving process reads bytes out of it, and TCP ensures that the bytes arrive reliably and in the same order they were written, without the application having to handle lost, duplicated, or reordered data. Because TCP is full-duplex, one connection carries two independent byte streams at once, one in each direction, so both applications can send and receive simultaneously. TCP also includes flow control, allowing the receiver to limit how much data the sender transmits.

TCP does not transmit individual bytes over the network. Instead, the sending host buffers bytes from the application until it has enough to fill a reasonably sized packet, then sends that packet as a TCP segment to the peer host. The receiving TCP puts the segment's data into a receive buffer, and the receiving application reads from that buffer at its own pace. Segments are the units TCP actually exchanges with its peer; the byte stream is the abstraction TCP presents to application processes.

5.2 Reliable Byte Stream (TCP)

In contrast to a simple demultiplexing protocol like UDP, a more sophisticated transport protocol is one that offers a reliable, connection-oriented, byte-stream service. Such a service has proven useful to a wide assortment of applications because it frees the application from having to worry about missing or reordered data. The Internet’s Transmission Control Protocol is probably the most widely used protocol of this type; it is also the most carefully tuned. It is for these two reasons that this section studies TCP in detail, although we identify and discuss alternative design choices at the end of the section.

In terms of the properties of transport protocols given in the problem statement at the start of this chapter, TCP guarantees the reliable, in-order delivery of a stream of bytes. It is a full-duplex protocol, meaning that each TCP connection supports a pair of byte streams, one flowing in each direction. It also includes a flow-control mechanism for each of these byte streams that allows the receiver to limit how much data the sender can transmit at a given time. Finally, like UDP, TCP supports a demultiplexing mechanism that allows multiple application programs on any given host to simultaneously carry on a conversation with their peers.

TCP is a byte-oriented protocol, which means that the sender writes bytes into a TCP connection and the receiver reads bytes out of the TCP connection. Although “byte stream” describes the service TCP offers to application processes, TCP does not, itself, transmit individual bytes over the Internet. Instead, TCP on the source host buffers enough bytes from the sending process to fill a reasonably sized packet and then sends this packet to its peer on the destination host. TCP on the destination host then empties the contents of the packet into a receive buffer, and the receiving process reads from this buffer at its leisure. This situation is illustrated in Figure 127, which, for simplicity, shows data flowing in only one direction. Remember that, in general, a single TCP connection supports byte streams flowing in both directions.

The packets exchanged between TCP peers in Figure 127 are called segments, since each one carries a segment of the byte stream. Each TCP segment contains the header schematically depicted in Figure 128. The relevance of most of these fields will become apparent throughout this section. For now, we simply introduce them.
